newsitem.title: FRANCE: French transport strikes winding down.
newsitem.headline: French transport strikes winding down.

text.p: Strikes by public transport drivers demanding early retirement and shorter working hours dogged French provincial cities for the seventh day on Wednesday but appeared to be crumbling in some towns.
The protests halted or disrupted buses, trams or underground railways in Marseille, Toulouse, Lille, Nice, Toulon, Cannes, Sete, Reims, Le Mans and other cities.
But buses were back on the streets of Evreux after an accord on gradual cuts in the working week to 35 from 39. Drivers in Marseille accepted a similar offer and voted to resume work on Thursday.
Unions and transport authorities in northern France agreed on shorter working hours but the strike went on as talks continued on early retirement.

In Clermont-Ferrand, the transport authority said some 15 percent of buses which were not in depots at the beginning of the conflict were running. In Dijon, bus services resumed after the transport authority appealed to the courts against strikers blocking depots.
In Toulouse, where the strike began three weeks ago, nine strikers accused of causing damages were suspended by transport authorities who hired private buses to replace halted services.

"This is totally illegal," Toulouse mayor Dominique Baudis told France-Inter radio. "Some 100 to 150 people are blocking the company, they have put buses across the street and punctured tyres. Most people in the company want to work."
The striking drivers want a working week of 35 hours instead of 39 with no loss of pay and retirement at 55 instead of 60.
The stoppages, which began with a one-day protest in about 20 major cities last Thursday, have spared Paris where drivers are already entitled to retire at 55.

The government bowed to truckers' demands for retirement at 55 after they blocked roads late last year. But it opposes extending the concession, saying it could bankrupt the pension system when post-war baby boomers start swelling the ranks of pensioners from 2005.
